==Problem 11==
Squares of side length 1, 1, 2, 3, and 5 are arranged to form the rectangle shown below. A curve is drawn by inscribing a quarter circle in each square and joining the quarter circles in order, from shortest to longest. What is the length of the curve?

==Solution 2 (No Fibonacci)==

For those who don't know Fibonacci's Spiral, One could see that between the two unit squares, the curvature is <imath> \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \pi (1) = \pi </imath>. For the unit 2 square, the curve is <imath> \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \pi (2) = \pi </imath>. For the unit three square, is is <imath> \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \pi (3) = \frac{3}{2} \pi </imath>. For the unit 5 square, we have <imath> \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \pi \cdot 5 = \frac{10}{4} \pi = \frac{5}{2} \pi </imath>. The length of the curve is <imath> 2\pi + \frac{8}{2} \pi = 2\pi + 4\pi = \boxed{6\pi} </imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 3 (Fibbonacci)==

For those who know Fibonacci's Spiral, the length of the curve <imath>L_n = \frac{\pi}{2} \sum_{k=1}^n F_k</imath> where <imath>F_k</imath> is the <imath>k</imath>th Fibonacci Number. Here, <imath>n</imath> is the number of squares the curve traverses. Then, <imath>L_5 = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot (12) = \boxed{6 \pi}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 4 (Straightforward)==


Note that the circumference of a quarter arc is <imath> \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \cdot \pi \cdot r</imath>
Which is the same thing as <imath> \frac {1}{2} \cdot \pi \cdot r </imath>

The first part of the spiral has a quarter circle with the radius of 5 and so the formula would be <cmath> \frac{1}{2} \cdot \pi \cdot 5 = \frac{5}{2}\pi </cmath>

The second part of the spiral has a quarter circle with the radius of 3 and so the formula is <cmath> \frac{1}{2} \cdot \pi \cdot 3 = \frac{3}{2}\pi </cmath>

The third part of the spiral has a quarter circle with the radius of 2 and so the formula is <cmath> \frac{1}{2} \cdot \pi\cdot2 = \pi </cmath>

The fourth and fifth part can be viewed as 2 quarter circles with radius 1, so they are essentially one semicircle with radius 1. The formula then would be <imath> \pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot r = \pi </imath> Therefore, it is just <imath> \pi </imath>. 

Adding them all up, we get <cmath> \frac{5}{2}\pi + \frac{3}{2}\pi + 1\pi +1\pi = \frac{8}{2}\pi + 2\pi = 6\pi </cmath>
Therefore our final answer is  <cmath> \boxed{6\pi}.</cmath>
